newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN launches aid operation for Iraqi Kurds in Iran.
newsitem.headline: UN launches aid operation for Iraqi Kurds in Iran.

text.p: The United Nations refugee agency said on Friday it was launching an emergency operation to provide shelter material and other relief goods to up to 40,000 Kurds from northern Iraq who have crossed into Iran.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) also said the Iranian Red Crescent and Ministry of Health officials were generally coping well with the sudden influx.
Landmines are the biggest threat facing displaced Kurds attempting to cross the border after a Baghdad-backed Kurdish faction took over northern Iraq, according to UNHCR spokesman Rupert Colville.
"We see some deficiencies in the (Iranian) operation, and hopefully we will try to plug in the gaps," he told a news briefing in Geneva.
"The assessment will be completed today. Then we will start moving," the spokesman added.

The Geneva-based agency gave no details of its operation, but said it had released cash from its emergency fund to buy and transport relief items. It may also redeploy staff and vehicles from its Afghan repatriation programme in eastern Iran.
Most of those who have managed to cross are sleeping in the open, due to a serious shortage of tents, the spokesman added.

UNHCR staff have reported that 30,000 Kurdish refugees are now in three border areas of northern Iran -- Sardasht (24,000), Cyramband (3,000) and Baghmagh (3,000). They were expected to report on numbers of refugees in Khermanshah later in the day.
"Our teams have now visited three major areas and verified the presence of 30,000 refugees," Colville said.
The spokesman described the situation as fluid, adding: "People are still coming in across the border but there has been quite a big return movement taking place, too."
"We believe the region has 35,000 to 40,000, or more or less what the Iranian government said on Wednesday."
On Wednesday, Iran said it was sheltering 39,000 Kurdish refugees and said it needed international assistance to cope.
Colville said: "We don't believe that at present there are more than 40,000 are in Iran...There don't appear to be big numbers immediately on the Iraqi border areas ready to cross."
"The biggest problem is mines," Colville said, referring to landmines on the Iraqi side of the militarily-sensitive border. "A lot of displaced people are afraid to step off the road."
In Sardasht, where the biggest makeshift camp of 23,000 people is located, only 400 tents have been erected, although another 600 are about to be set up, according to UNHCR.
Some cases of flu and diarrhoea have been reported among the refugees in Sardasht, but Iranian medical teams are circulating.
The Iranian Red Crescent has distributed bread, potatoes, rice and biscuits in Sardasht, "but they don't have sufficient quantities at present", according to the UNHCR spokesman.
UNHCR has praised Tehran's "track record" in giving asylum to millions of desperate refugees from Afghanistan and Iraq starting in the 1980s.
Iran is currently home to two million refugees, 1.4 million from Afghanistan and 600,000 from Iraq -- making it the largest host country in the world, according to UNHCR.
